blocks.x: Core definitions

Protein A polymer of amino acid monomers that folds into a three-dimensional structure determined by its amino acid sequence — the agents of biological function and the expressions of genetic information.
Amino acid residue What remains of an amino acid after the release of a water molecule during peptide bond formation.

Proteins are the most versatile macromolecules in organisms: they catalyse reactions, transport and store other molecules (e.g. oxygen), provide mechanical support and immune protection, generate movement, transmit nerve impulses, and control cell proliferation and differentiation. Some proteins are rigid structural scaffolds; others are flexible hinges, springs and levers.
Amino acids→ Peptide bond→ Polypeptide→ Folded protein→ Biological function

sections.title: Anatomy of a typical amino acid

blocks.x: Building blocks
Every protein is built from the same 20-letter alphabet of monomers. Their shared backbone and variable side chains (R groups) give proteins their enormous functional diversity.
Anatomy of a typical amino acid

Central to every amino acid is a tetrahedral alpha (α) carbon, covalently linked to an amino group (–NH₃⁺), a carboxyl group (–COO⁻), a hydrogen, and a variable side chain (R group) that gives each amino acid its identity. Because the α-carbon is chiral, amino acids exist as D- and L-enantiomers — proteins are built almost exclusively from L-amino acids.
Classification by side-chain polarity
All amino acids except proline have free α-amino and α-carboxyl groups. The most useful classification is based on the polarity of the R group:
Nonpolar
Glycine, Alanine, Valine, Leucine, Isoleucine, Methionine, Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, Proline
Polar, neutral
Serine, Threonine, Cysteine, Tyrosine, Asparagine, Glutamine
Acidic (− at pH 7)
Aspartate (Asp), Glutamate (Glu) — carry a net negative charge at neutral pH
Basic (+ at pH 7)
Lysine (Lys), Arginine (Arg), Histidine (His) — carry a net positive charge at neutral pH
Essential, semi-essential & non-essential amino acids

blocks.title: Essential amino acids: why the body can't make them

items: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised in the body of higher animals and must be provided in the diet.

The inability to synthesise them may be due to the absence of (1) the corresponding α-keto acid of the amino acid, and (2) the enzyme involved in transamination — a specific transaminase (uses pyridoxal phosphate).
Young animals fail to grow on diets deficient in even one essential amino acid. Prolonged deficiency of amino acids leads to kwashiorkor, with low plasma protein and haemoglobin levels.
Histidine and arginine are semi-essential — the body can synthesise them, but not adequately.
Proteins from cereals are poor in lysine; proteins from legumes are low in methionine.

blocks.x: Uncommon amino acids & amino acids not in proteins
Rare, in-protein residues

Hydroxylysine & hydroxyproline occur mainly in collagen and gelatin. Thyroxine and 3,3′,5-triiodothyronine are iodinated amino acids found only in thyroglobulin, released as thyroid hormones. Muscle proteins contain methylated residues (methylhistidine, ε-N-methyllysine, ε-N,N,N-trimethyllysine). γ-Carboxyglutamic acid occurs in blood-clotting proteins; pyroglutamic acid occurs in bacteriorhodopsin (Halobacterium salinarum). Regulatory proteins are reversibly phosphorylated on Ser/Thr/Tyr –OH groups. Aminoadipic acid occurs in corn proteins; N-methylarginine and N-acetyllysine occur in histones.
Biochemically important, but not in proteins

GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid), from glutamate decarboxylation, is a potent neurotransmitter. Histamine (from histidine) and serotonin (from tryptophan) are neurotransmitters/regulators. β-Alanine is found in the peptides carnosine and anserine, and is a component of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) in coenzyme A. Epinephrine (adrenaline), derived from tyrosine, is a key hormone. Penicillamine is a constituent of the penicillin antibiotics.
Chemistry & methods
All amino acids share reactive α-carboxyl and α-amino groups, and the peptide bond that joins them. Their side-chain chemistry also underlies how they are detected, separated and identified.
Formation of the peptide bond

The crucial feature that allows amino acids to polymerise into peptides and proteins is the existence of their two identifying chemical groups — the amino (–NH₃⁺) and carboxyl (–COO⁻) groups. The carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of the next, releasing a molecule of water and forming a covalent CO–NH peptide bond. Repetition of this reaction builds long polymers, with a free amino end (N-terminus) and a free carboxyl end (C-terminus).

Amino acid 1
(–COOH)+ Amino acid 2
(–NH₃⁺)→ Peptide bond
(– H₂O)→ Dipeptide

blocks.title: Reasons the chemical reactivity of amino acids matters

items: Proteins can be chemically modified by exploiting the reactivity of specific side chains.
The detection and quantification of amino acids and proteins often depends on reactions specific to one or more amino acids, producing colour changes or other measurable quantities.
Most importantly, the biological functions of proteins depend on the behaviour and reactivity of specific R groups.

blocks.x: Carboxyl and amino group reactions
Reacts with ammonia and amines to give unsubstituted (RCONH₂) and substituted (RCONHR′) amides. Readily forms esters and acid chlorides. Repetition of the reaction gives polymerisation.
Free amino groups react with aldehydes to form Schiff bases, and can be acylated with acid anhydrides and acid halides to give substituted amides.
The ninhydrin reaction

Ninhydrin (triketohydrindene hydrate) is a strong oxidising agent that causes oxidative deamination of the α-amino function, producing an aldehyde, ammonia, CO₂, and hydrindantin. Ammonia then reacts with hydrindantin and a second ninhydrin molecule to form Ruhemann's Purple, quantified spectrophotometrically at 570 nm; the appearance of CO₂ can also be monitored.

blocks.title: Specific reactions of amino acid side chains

items: Cysteine residues react with one another to form disulphide (cystine) linkages, and with reagents such as N-ethylmaleimide.
Cysteines react with iodoacetate to yield S-carboxymethyl cysteine derivatives, and with acrylonitrile.
Ellman's reagent (DTNB, 5,5′-dithiobis-2-nitrobenzoic acid) reacts with free thiols to release a thiol anion with λmax = 412 nm, a common assay for free –SH groups.
p-Hydroxymercuribenzoate also reacts specifically with cysteine thiols.
Lysine's ε-amino group reacts with aldehydes to form Schiff bases.

blocks.x: Spectroscopic properties of amino acids

No amino acid absorbs visible light, but several absorb ultraviolet radiation, and all absorb in the infrared region. The aromatic amino acids — phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan — show strong UV absorption above 250 nm, useful for spectroscopic determinations. They also show weak fluorescence, and tryptophan additionally exhibits phosphorescence — properties especially useful in studying protein structure and dynamics.
Separation & analysis of amino acid mixtures

Amino acid separations rely on differences in partition properties (the tendency to associate with one phase over another) and electrical charge. In partition methods, molecules flow through a medium with two phases (solid-liquid, liquid-liquid or gas-liquid); the ratio of amino acid concentration between the two phases is its partition coefficient.

Solutes pass through columns of a porous, charged solid support (resin); as the eluant flows, amino acids separate into discrete, sequentially eluting bands. Other essential methods include gas chromatography (GC), liquid chromatography (LC) and HPLC.
Acid hydrolysis of proteins

Peptide bonds are hydrolysed by strong acid or base. Acid hydrolysis (typically 6 M HCl, 110 °C, for 24/48/72 hours in sealed vials) occurs without racemisation and is less destructive to Ser, Thr, Arg and Cys than alkaline treatment, making it the method of choice for determining amino acid composition. However, tryptophan is destroyed by acid and must be estimated separately; serine and threonine are slowly destroyed; hydrophobic residues (valine, isoleucine) are slowly hydrolysed. The acid-labile amides of asparagine and glutamine release free ammonium and become aspartic/glutamic acid — reported as Asx and Glx since the original proportions cannot be recovered from the data.
From chain to machine
Amino acids polymerise into peptides, then polypeptides, then fold into the four hierarchical levels of structure that give each protein its unique, functional shape.
Peptide classification & polypeptide chains
By chain length
Dipeptides contain 2 residues, tripeptides 3, and so on. Chains with more than 12 and fewer than 20 residues are oligopeptides; chains exceeding several dozen residues are called polypeptides.
By subunit composition

A protein with one chain is monomeric; more than one chain is multimeric. Multimers of one kind of chain are homomultimeric (e.g. an α₂ homodimer); of different chains, heteromultimeric (e.g. haemoglobin's α₂β₂).
Amino acid sequence: the N- to C-terminal read

The unique characteristic of each protein is the distinctive sequence of amino acid residues in its polypeptide chain(s). This sequence is a form of genetic information, encoded by the DNA sequence, and is read by convention from the N-terminal end through to the C-terminal end. With 20 possible amino acids at every position, the number of unique sequences possible is astronomically large.
Architecture of protein molecules
Proteins fall into three global classes based on shape and solubility:
Fibrous
Simple, regular, linear structures serving structural roles; typically insoluble in water or dilute salt (e.g. collagen).
Globular
Roughly spherical; hydrophobic side chains pack into the interior, hydrophilic side chains face the solvent — usually very soluble (e.g. myoglobin, cytosolic enzymes).
Membrane
Associated with membranes; hydrophobic residues face outward into the nonpolar bilayer. Insoluble in water but solubilised by detergents; fewer hydrophilic residues than cytosolic proteins.
Hierarchical organisation of protein structure

1PrimaryThe linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds — the "one-dimensional" identity of the protein. 2SecondaryRegular, repeating local folding patterns stabilised by hydrogen bonds — chiefly the α-helix and the β-pleated sheet. 3TertiaryThe overall 3-D folding of a single polypeptide chain, packing secondary-structure elements together into a compact globular or fibrous form. 4QuaternaryThe spatial arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits into one functional multimeric protein assembly.
Example: functional haemoglobin is a quaternary assembly of four subunits (two α, two β), each individually folded to the tertiary level.
Simple vs. conjugated proteins
Many proteins are made of amino acids alone — but many others carry a non-protein chemical group as an integral part of their structure and function.
Simple protein Contains only amino acids and no other chemical groups — e.g. ribonuclease and the contractile protein actin.

Conjugated protein / prosthetic group Contains a non-amino-acid chemical constituent as an integral part of its structure. If that nonprotein part is crucial to function, it is called a prosthetic group. If it is not covalently linked, it can be removed by denaturing the protein.
Conjugated proteins are classified according to the chemical nature of their non-amino-acid component.
Representative conjugated proteins

c: Ribosomes (RNA, ~60%), tobacco mosaic virus (RNA), adenovirus (DNA), HIV-1 (RNA)
Ferritin (iron, ~35%), alcohol dehydrogenase (zinc), cytochrome oxidase (Cu & Fe), nitrogenase (Mo & Fe)
Haemoglobin, cytochrome c, catalase, nitrate reductase
Succinate dehydrogenase (FAD), NADH dehydrogenase (FMN), sulfite reductase

items: Contain carbohydrate; proteins destined for an extracellular location are characteristically glycoproteins.
Fibronectin and proteoglycans are essential components of the extracellular matrix surrounding cells in most animal tissues.
Immunoglobulin G is the principal antibody species circulating free in blood plasma.
Most membrane proteins are glycosylated on their extracellular segments.

Lipoproteins (e.g. blood plasma HDL/LDL) function primarily in transporting lipids to sites of active membrane synthesis. Serum LDL is used clinically as an index of susceptibility to vascular disease.
Nucleoproteins play roles in storing and transmitting genetic information; ribosomes are sites of protein synthesis, and viral particles and chromosomes are protein–nucleic acid complexes.

Phosphoproteins have phosphate esterified to the –OH of serine, threonine or tyrosine residues; casein brings essential phosphorus to a growing infant, and phosphorylation regulates protein activity/inactivity states.
Flavoproteins require flavin (FAD and/or FMN) for oxidoreductase activity.
Metalloproteins are either metal storage forms (ferritin) or enzymes in which the metal participates catalytically.

Haemoproteins are a subclass of metalloproteins whose prosthetic group is haem (iron protoporphyrin IX); because haem-containing proteins have so many prominent biological functions, they are considered a class by themselves.

blocks.x: Function follows form
Proteins are grouped into functional classes reflecting the extraordinary breadth of roles they play in the cell — and, once identified, must be purified from thousands of others.
Biological functions of proteins

items: Enzymes are the largest class of proteins — catalysts that accelerate biological reaction rates, sometimes by as much as 10¹⁶-fold over the uncatalysed rate. Each enzyme is specific to a particular metabolic reaction (e.g. ribonuclease, trypsin, alcohol dehydrogenase, catalase).

Regulatory proteins do not perform a chemical transformation themselves but regulate other proteins' ability to function. Insulin regulates glucose metabolism; pituitary somatotropin and thyrotropin are also protein hormones. Repressors are negative control elements of gene expression.

Transport proteins move specific substances from place to place: haemoglobin carries O₂ from lungs to tissues; serum albumin carries fatty acids. Membrane transporters move metabolites across permeability barriers.

Storage proteins provide a reservoir of an essential nutrient — often nitrogen. Ovalbumin (egg white) and casein (milk) supply nitrogen to developing embryos/infants. Seeds may be up to 60% storage protein (zein in corn, phaseolin in peas). Ferritin binds iron — a single 460 kD molecule binds up to 4,500 iron atoms.
Contractile and motile proteins enable movement: actin and myosin form contractile systems; tubulin builds microtubules for the mitotic spindle, flagella and cilia.

Structural proteins give strength and protection: α-keratins form hair, horns and nails; collagen forms inelastic fibrils in bone, tendon and cartilage; elastin's cross-linked monomers let ligaments stretch in two dimensions.

Scaffold (adapter) proteins have modular domains that recognise structural elements in other proteins: SH2 domains bind phosphorylated tyrosine, SH3 domains bind proline-rich regions, PH domains bind membranes, and PDZ domains bind a protein's C-terminal amino acid.

Protective/exploitive proteins defend or exploit: immunoglobulins (antibodies) recognise and neutralise foreign invaders; thrombin and fibrinogen prevent blood loss; antifreeze proteins protect Arctic/Antarctic fish; snake and bee venom proteins and the plant toxin ricin deter predation; bacteria produce toxins such as diphtheria and cholera toxin.

Exotic proteins perform unusual roles: monellin (African plant) is a natural sweetener; resilin gives insect wing hinges their elasticity; marine molluscs secrete glue proteins to attach to hard surfaces.

blocks.x: Protein separation methods

Because cells contain thousands of different proteins, the central problem for protein chemists is to purify one specific protein. Proteins are separated and purified based on two physical properties: size and electrical charge — or directly, via affinity purification strategies that exploit a protein's biological function.
By size
Size-exclusion chromatography, ultrafiltration, and ultracentrifugation.
By charge
Ion exchange chromatography, electrophoresis, and solubility-based separation.

items: Proteins show minimal solubility at their isoelectric point — the pH at which net charge is zero — because electrostatic repulsion between molecules is minimal, favouring precipitation.
Ionic strength profoundly affects solubility. At low salt (<0.5 M), ions shield protein charges from one another, reducing protein–protein interactions and increasing solubility — salting-in.
At high salt (>1 M), salt ions compete with the protein for water of solvation; the protein becomes insoluble — salting-out.
Exposed nonpolar side chains at a soluble protein's surface give it a degree of partial hydrophobicity that also influences these behaviours.
